episodes.title: How Inflation and Fiscal Policy Are Driving US Treasury Markets
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Goldman Sachs' head of US Treasuries and inflation trading discusses the August 12 CPI print, the Fed's dual mandate tension, heavy Treasury supply/fiscal deficits, and record-high real yields. For an EM trader, this is a pure read on the US rates and dollar backdrop that anchors global risk appetite and carry trades.

**Key points**
- Core CPI printed 0.215% m/m, seen as "down the middle"; softer services inflation implies an even softer core PCE read-through, prompting forecast downgrades.
- September FOMC pricing eased to ~9bp of cuts priced after the data; PPI (Wednesday) and retail sales (Friday) are the next catalysts before the meeting.
- July payrolls were negative for the first time in a while, but 3- and 12-month average job growth (~20-30k/month) alongside an unchanged unemployment rate over 12 months means the labor market is not driving Fed policy — inflation is.
- 10-year Treasury auction was the highest-yielding since 2007 yet was smoothly digested, helped by the soft CPI; a 30-year auction follows Thursday.
- Heavy Treasury issuance plus $250bn (potentially $400bn next year) of AI-infrastructure-related corporate credit supply is pushing term premium structurally higher.
- Real yields are historically elevated (~2.5% 10y, ~3% 30y tips), levels rarely sustained since the GFC, seen as attractive for long-horizon investors and portfolio diversification.
- Preferred trade: a curve steepener, anchored by a front end/belly that's fully priced for Fed action, against a back end facing ongoing term-premium and supply headwinds.

**FX / rates implications**
- Elevated and rising UST term premium plus persistent fiscal supply pressure is a structural headwind for global duration and keeps a floor under US real yields, a modest drag on EM carry trades funded via cheap USD financing.
- A steady-to-softer inflation path supports near-term USD/UST stability, but any hawkish Fed reaction-function shift (post-Chair Worsh's dovish July comments) could push long yields and the dollar higher, pressuring EM FX.
- No EM-specific catalysts discussed, but the broad risk backdrop (recession-tail steepener thesis) is relevant to EM rates positioning as a hedge.

**Watch list**
- PPI report (Wednesday) and 30-year Treasury auction (Thursday).
- Retail sales data (Friday).
- FOMC minutes from the July meeting, next week, for read-through to the September decision.

episodes.title: Through the noise: Geopolitical stalemate, cooling jobs and inflation
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Standard Chartered's weekly macro podcast covers the Middle East stalemate's effect on energy prices, cooling US inflation/employment data, and diverging central bank paths for the Fed, ECB and BoJ, alongside equity and credit market views. The read-through is mostly global/DM-focused with limited direct EM Asia/LATAM specifics, but the USD, rates and risk-sentiment channels matter for EM positioning.

**Key points**
- US July headline CPI slowed to 3.4% y/y, core CPI to 2.5% (lowest since 2021); PPI deteriorated to 4.7% y/y.
- Non-farm payrolls unexpectedly contracted by 23,000, with May/June revised down, suggesting spring hiring momentum has faded.
- Base case: Fed holds rates through year-end; ECB and BoJ each seen delivering one more hike this year.
- 30-year UST auction (Aug 13) priced at the highest yield level since 2007, reflecting fiscal concerns.
- US high-yield spreads (~266bp) near 15-year tights (4th percentile), but yield (~7.26%) at 69th percentile; default rate ~2% vs 3-3.5% long-term average.
- RBA seen hawkish, supportive of AUD; forecasts 0.74/0.75 vs USD at 3/12 months; gold-AUD correlation at 0.82 (3-month) vs 0.59 (3-year).
- Constructive on China tech equities amid AI-driven IPO momentum and Hang Seng Tech Index expansion from 30 to 50 constituents.

**FX / rates implications**
- Softer US data + Fed on hold caps front/belly UST yields, but fiscal-driven long-end pressure persists — a mixed USD signal for EM carry trades.
- Prospective ECB and BoJ hikes vs a paused Fed could narrow rate differentials, a modest USD headwind supportive of EM FX broadly.
- Persistent Middle East risk keeps European gas prices elevated, a tail risk for global inflation and risk sentiment relevant to EM risk appetite.
- China tech/AI IPO enthusiasm and constructive China growth view support CNH/CNY sentiment and broader EM Asia risk tone.

**Watch list**
- Further US CPI/payrolls prints and Fed year-end policy signals.
- ECB and BoJ meetings for confirmation of expected additional hikes.
- European natural gas prices as an inflation transmission risk.
- US Treasury long-end auctions for fiscal-driven yield pressure.

episodes.title: Retiree benefits bump, credit repayment slump, and a dating app in the dumps
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This Indicator of the Week episode covers three unrelated US data points: the July CPI-W inflation reading used to set Social Security's 2027 cost-of-living adjustment, rising serious delinquency in US credit card debt, and Bumble's collapsing paid user base. None directly concerns EM Asia or LATAM FX/rates, but the CPI and consumer-credit data add texture to the US inflation and consumer-health picture that ultimately feeds into Fed policy expectations.

**Key points**
- CPI-W (Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers index), used since 1973 to set Social Security's COLA, rose 3.4% year-over-year in July; the final COLA figure is confirmed in October.
- AARP projects a 3.5% Social Security COLA for 2027 (~$73/month extra for average retirees); the Senior Citizens League projects 3.6%, which would be the largest increase in four years.
- 12.8% of US credit card debt is now seriously delinquent (90+ days past due) per a New York Fed report — the highest since around the Great Recession, though the pace of new delinquencies has been stable; auto loan and mortgage delinquencies are also rising.
- Bumble's paying users fell 16% over 12 months; Bumble stock is down ~95% and Match Group (Tinder) down ~70% over five years, while Grindr is up ~50% since its 2021 IPO. Both Bumble and Match Group are pivoting to in-person meetup features to reverse declines.

**FX / rates implications**
- No direct EM Asia/LATAM read-through; this is US domestic CPI/consumer-credit color rather than a market-moving headline print (the headline CPI-U, not CPI-W, drives Fed pricing and DXY/UST moves).
- Rising US consumer delinquencies (credit card, auto, mortgage) are a soft signal of US household stress that could eventually feed into growth/Fed-cut narratives relevant to USD and broad EM risk appetite, but the transmission here is indirect and not quantified in growth terms.

**Watch list**
- Official Social Security COLA announcement due in October, based on final CPI-W data.
- Ongoing New York Fed household debt/delinquency data for signs of broader US consumer credit stress.

episodes.title: The Week Ahead – Light on data and low on clarity
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Nomura's Week Ahead covers a light global data calendar but several EM-relevant central bank and data events: Bank Indonesia's first policy decision under acting governor Destry Damayanti following the shock resignation of Perry Warjiyo, Thailand's Q2 GDP, and China's July activity data alongside fiscal stimulus prospects. US CPI/PPI and the upcoming FOMC minutes are also covered, framing the broader Fed path that anchors EM rates and FX.

**Key points**
- US CPI rose 0.215% m/m, close to consensus; combined with PPI, Nomura forecasts core PCE at 0.234% m/m, near the Fed's comfort threshold; weak NFP reinforces a cooling growth narrative supporting a Fed pause for the rest of the year.
- China: July industrial production expected at 5.0% y/y (vs 5.3% in June) on strong exports (+24% y/y), but retail sales (+1.5% y/y) and fixed asset investment (-8% y/y) remain weak; Nomura cut Q3 GDP forecast to 4.3% y/y from 4.5%. Big fiscal stimulus unlikely before September/October, impact mostly Q4.
- Bank Indonesia expected to hold rates at 5.75% under new acting governor Destry Damayanti, who is likely to signal policy continuity, continued macroprudential easing, and double-digit money supply targeting.
- Thailand Q2 GDP expected to slow sharply to 1.8% y/y (from 2.8% in Q1) on weak manufacturing and tourism; supports Bank of Thailand staying on hold all year.
- Gold trading above $4,300 on structural central bank buying and rate/geopolitical uncertainty; Brent crude near $90.

**FX / rates implications**
- IDR: BI hold plus continuity signal under new leadership should be modestly IDR-supportive; watch for any dovish tilt from macroprudential easing.
- THB: Weak Q2 GDP print reinforces BoT-on-hold view, capping THB upside; energy-shock vulnerability is a THB-specific drag versus regional peers.
- CNY: Soft demand-side data and delayed fiscal stimulus (Q4 impact) argue for continued PBoC accommodation bias and limited near-term CNY strength.
- USD/UST: A Fed pause narrative (supported by CPI/NFP) and dovish FOMC minutes expectations are broadly USD-negative/EM-FX supportive; long-end UST uncertainty flagged as a key risk factor for gold and broader risk sentiment.

**Watch list**
- Bank Indonesia rate decision (expected hold at 5.75%) under acting governor Destry Damayanti.
- China July activity data: industrial production, retail sales, fixed asset investment.
- FOMC minutes for hawk/dove divide and rate-hike threshold clues.
- Thailand Q2 GDP and BoT decision later this month.
- UK July CPI and Riksbank/Norges Bank rate paths.

episodes.title: A Historic El Niño Is Coming That Could Cost the World Trillions
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Odd Lots interviews Dartmouth climate scientist Justin Mankin on a forecast record-breaking El Niño (advisory since June 2026, peaking Dec-Feb, winding down Feb-Mar 2027), with sell-side desks (Citi on Thailand rates, Morgan Stanley on BoE, Bank of America on EM FX) already flagging it. Relevant background for EM macro trades given El Niño's documented drag on growth trajectories, not just price levels, and its links to monsoon timing, diesel subsidies and agri/commodity supply chains.

**Key points**
- Rooney (Relative Oceanic Niño Index) forecasts exceeding the 3.3 threshold for the first time on record; models converge on the strongest El Niño since at least 1950.
- Research (Callahan/Mankin, Science 2023) found El Niño causes permanent growth-trajectory shocks, not one-off level effects: the 1997-98 El Niño's initially estimated $36bn cost ballooned to an estimated $5.7 trillion in cumulative global losses by 2003.
- This event is projected to cause $10-14 trillion in global economic losses over five years, with only ~70% considered in-sample/predictable from historical data.
- El Niño already delayed the 2026 South Asian monsoon onset, historically linked to Indian diesel prices, farmer distress and local election outcomes.
- Peru's economy (mining, port logistics via road washouts) is cited as a classic high-teleconnection casualty; global fertilizer supply (~40% still constrained by the Russia/Ukraine war) compounds agri-price risk.

**FX / rates implications**
- Thin, indirect read-through: inflationary/growth-drag risk for India (monsoon/diesel channel, INR, RBI policy) and Peru (mining/export disruption, PEN); broader EM Asia agri-exporters and commodity-linked LATAM currencies face tail risk from a record El Niño layered on existing warming trends.
- No explicit Fed, DXY, UST, or China commentary in this episode.

**Watch list**
- El Niño peak strength and Rooney readings through winter 2026-27; NOAA CPC updates.
- South Asian monsoon progression and any diesel-subsidy/political flashpoints in India.
- Sell-side EM FX and rates notes (Citi, Morgan Stanley, BofA) continuing to price El Niño into Thailand rates, EM currency and BoE outlooks.

episodes.title: Global FX: Debate Corner
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
JPMorgan FX strategists debate three live calls: the dollar's direction, whether low-yielding DM cyclicals (SEK, CAD) are due a comeback, and what it will take to stabilize the yen. The team recently trimmed its bullish dollar conviction to neutral tactically but retains a bullish bias structurally, while flagging carry as the dominant, less exciting theme actually driving FX returns.

**Key points**
- Dollar bulls cite cheap real yield spreads, accelerating ISM manufacturing, low jobless claims, and labor-supply constraints (immigration, retirees) as inflationary risks; bears note the labor-market turn that drove the May-July ~100bp rates repricing has faded, with wage growth at cycle lows (~3% real) and core PCE trending softer barring this month's hot 0.32% print.
- Lisa Cook Fed-independence risk flagged as underappreciated; dollar has shown renewed negative sensitivity to term premium/twist-steepening since the FOMC press conference.
- Global FX carry baskets have returned 6-12% YTD, described as the real driver of FX P&L versus the binary dollar debate.
- SEK: growth/inflation upgrades look better but conditions aren't ripe for outright bullishness without falling US yields or equity momentum shift; CAD: strong Q2 data offset by BoC seeing excess capacity and unresolved USMCA Section 338 tariff deadline next week.
- Yen: BoJ pricing ~3 hikes over next year; desk argues even 2% policy rates may not be enough given yen cheapness versus other funders; CHF preferred over JPY as a funding currency.

**FX / rates implications**
- Dollar bias stays bullish but range-bound (hawkish Fed repricing capped near 35-40bp, worth only ~1% on DXY); downside better anchored than upside is open given Fed pricing already low.
- Dollar-yen faces continued upward pressure absent Fed cuts or a credible BoJ acceleration plus fiscal/GPIF/NISA flow support; joint MOF/BoJ intervention seen as necessary but insufficient alone.
- Low-yielding cyclicals (SEK, CAD) remain vulnerable while yielding less than USD; single-factor, carry-dominated market limits upside despite improving bottom-up stories.

**Watch list**
- Jackson Hole as a potential venue for Fed to reaffirm inflation commitment.
- USMCA Section 338 tariff deadline next week for CAD.
- Further BoJ/MOF intervention signals, GPIF/life insurer bond-buying flow measures, and JGB curve flattening as yen stabilizers.
- Lisa Cook Supreme Court legal proceedings and any risk premium attached to UST long end.

episodes.title: 269: The Biggest Themes of 2026 So Far: How AI, Geopolitics and Digital Assets Are Reshaping Portfolios
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A BlackRock "The Bid" retrospective episode stitches together 2026's recurring investment themes — geopolitics, AI/energy, market concentration, portfolio construction, digital assets, tokenization and Asia — into one narrative arc. It's a strategic/thematic overview rather than a market-moving data episode, but it synthesizes framing that macro traders may find useful for context.

**Key points**
- BlackRock's Tom Donnellan (BII Chairman) called 2025-26 a potential "hinge moment" akin to 1945, 1973-74 oil embargo, or 1989/91 Soviet collapse — a structural geopolitical/economic shift.
- AI is reframed as a physical, power-hungry infrastructure story: rising to "yottaflop" compute, straining grids, gas, nuclear and data centers (guest Will Sue).
- S&P 500 concentration is at a historical extreme — top 10 stocks are ~40% of the index (Ibrahim Kanan), undermining assumed diversification.
- BlackRock's Vivek Paul argued macro anchors (inflation stability, fiscal paths, policy predictability) no longer hold as they used to, requiring more dynamic, granular portfolio construction.
- Asia now represents ~40% of global GDP (up from 20% in 1990) and over 50% of listed companies worldwide (Arty Angara), reinforcing it as a core, not peripheral, allocation.
- Digital assets/Bitcoin discussed as a non-sovereign, decentralized asset class with unique risk/return drivers (Robbie Mitchnick); tokenization framed as the next market-infrastructure technology (Rob Goldstein).
- Jean Boivin introduced "polyfrication" — the need to hold multiple plausible macro scenarios simultaneously rather than a single base case.

**FX / rates implications**
- No direct FX/rates calls, but the "multiple plausible futures" framing and fading macro anchors argue for wider EM scenario ranges and less reliance on historical inflation/fiscal correlations when positioning carry trades.
- Asia's rising structural weight in global portfolios supports the broader case for sustained EM Asia capital-flow relevance.
- AI-driven power/infrastructure demand is a long-run theme for commodities (gas, copper, uranium) relevant to LATAM/EM commodity exporters, though not quantified here.

**Watch list**
- BlackRock's ongoing thematic content (energy/AI, tokenization, Asia allocation) for follow-on portfolio-construction guidance.
- Continued S&P 500 concentration trends as a risk-sentiment/diversification signal.

episodes.title: Record temperatures, record bonuses
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A GlobalCapital podcast covers three DCM/IB themes: markets' muted reaction to European/US heatwaves and wildfires despite record equity highs, the resumption of SSA benchmark bond issuance ("mini-January") after the summer lull, and a hiring boom for medium-term note (MTN) bankers alongside record investment-banking bonus forecasts. This is trade-press/DCM color rather than direct EM FX/rates content, with only tangential macro read-throughs.

**Key points**
- Despite Rhine/Danube drought (Romania and Hungary forced to curtail nuclear power output from cooling-water shortages), Eurostoxx 50 and S&P 500 hit record highs Thursday with credit spreads and yields unmoved; a securitization story flags rising wildfire risk to mortgage-backed collateral (insurance withdrawal risk) in UK/Netherlands MBS markets.
- SSA issuance resumes next week (KfW, EIB, Finland, German agencies) after a five-week lull, dubbed "mini-January"; issuers are considering pre-funding into 2027 given US midterms, Fed meeting uncertainty (30% hike odds priced for the last meeting, 50% for September), and French political/budget risk.
- Dollar SSA spreads continue grinding toward UST levels (a 10y World Bank priced 2.7bp over Treasuries in May, tighter in secondary and in 5y); "de-Treasurization" theme cited as Asian real-money investors diversify slightly from Treasuries while staying in USD via SSA credits.
- Record ECM/M&A bonus pools forecast (Johnson Associates survey) on SpaceX IPO-scale deal activity; US bankers seeing $5-10m bonuses (vs $2-5m two years ago), driven by US banks' scale advantage over European peers; MTN banker hiring is intense amid a talent shortage.

**FX / rates implications**
- Minimal direct EM read-through; the Fed-meeting uncertainty (Sept FOMC ~50% hike odds per bankers cited) and French political-risk-into-2026-elections theme are the closest links to broader rates/risk sentiment relevant to G10/EM carry trades.

**Watch list**
- Fed September FOMC meeting (bankers cite ~50% probability of a hike).
- SSA primary issuance volumes and USD/EUR spread-to-Treasury tightening next week.
- French budget and pre-election bond-market volatility into 2027 presidential elections.

episodes.title: Black Sea headline risk & wheat volatility
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A McKinney-Flavell commodity analyst discusses the run-up in wheat prices driven by Black Sea headline risk, as renewed Russia-Ukraine attacks on port infrastructure disrupt grain exports. Russia and Ukraine together account for nearly a third of global wheat exports, so escalation is being priced as a supply-disruption risk even though underlying crops are large and undamaged.

**Key points**
- Kansas City hard red winter wheat has risen 17-30 cents/bushel on fresh Black Sea attack headlines, now around $7.50/bushel; Chicago wheat near $7/bushel.
- Ukraine has attacked Russian deep-sea ports including forcing a shutdown of the Novorossiysk corridor (~25% of Russia's wheat exports); Russia's export pace is reportedly down ~75% in the first two weeks of August.
- A Turkey-brokered truce proposal from Ukraine was denied/rejected by Russia this week, extending the uncertainty.
- US wheat remains uncompetitive globally — physical sales/shipments are down 30% y/y, and prices would need to fall roughly $1/bushel to be competitive internationally.
- Ukraine warns European-bound exports could fall up to 50% if the conflict persists.
- Australia's wheat crop outlook has improved on timely rainfall despite earlier El Niño-driven dryness concerns and acreage cuts.

**FX / rates implications**
- Limited direct EM FX/rates read-through, but sustained agri-commodity inflation (wheat) is a modest upside risk to food-CPI in EM importer economies, relevant background for central bank inflation trackers (RBI, BSP, Banxico) if it persists.
- A prolonged Black Sea conflict is a geopolitical risk-off input that can support safe-haven USD and pressure broader risk sentiment, indirectly touching EM carry trades.

**Watch list**
- Further Black Sea port attacks or any truce/de-escalation headlines between Russia and Ukraine.
- Russia's wheat export pace recovery (currently ~75% below normal).
- Whether KC wheat pulls back toward the $6.75-6.80 range, seen as a potential buy-the-dip level by the analyst.
- Australia's crop progress through the peak of the current El Niño.

episodes.title: As Older Workers Retire, Labor Costs Ease
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
PIMCO's Tiffany Wilding examines an unusual divergence in US labor data: the unemployment rate has fallen even as the employment-to-population ratio drops, a pattern with no precedent since 1949. The analysis argues labor supply contraction, not demand strength, is driving lower unemployment, complicating the Fed's read on labor market slack and its policy calibration.

**Key points**
- US unemployment sits at 4.1% in July 2026, below its late-2025 peak, but labor force participation has fallen a full percentage point since December 2025 to its lowest level outside COVID since 1976.
- Under an unchanged-participation-rate scenario, unemployment would be roughly 5.6%, the highest since 2021 — implying real labor market slack is greater than headline unemployment suggests.
- A BLS population data revision explains under 40% of the participation decline; the rest reflects retirements among older, higher-income workers plus falling job-finding rates among prime-age and college-educated workers (5% now vs 6-8% historically), possibly tied to AI-driven labor reallocation.
- Wage growth and unit labor costs are easing, indicating labor is not a source of inflationary pressure despite the confusing signals.
- Taylor rules using unemployment may overestimate labor market tightness; substituting employment-to-population gaps prescribes policy rates 100bp lower than unemployment-based rules.

**FX / rates implications**
- Confirms the Fed has room to view current policy as appropriately calibrated rather than needing to tighten further on labor-cost inflation fears, supportive of a dovish-leaning Fed reaction function — a modest USD headwind and constructive for EM carry trades broadly.
- Reduced Fed hawkish risk lowers UST yield upside, generally favorable for EM Asia and LATAM local-rates duration and FX carry (INR, IDR, MXN, BRL) via lower US real rate anchor.
- If labor supply-driven unemployment declines mask true slack, markets may underprice Fed cutting scope, a theme relevant to DXY and EM FX positioning into upcoming FOMC meetings.

**Watch list**
- Upcoming US payrolls, participation rate, and wage/unit labor cost prints for confirmation of the supply-driven narrative.
- Fed communications on which labor market gauge (unemployment vs employment-population ratio) informs the reaction function ahead of FOMC decisions.
- Further BLS data revisions that could reshape the labor supply/demand picture.
